title: What is known about 1RB1LE_0RC---_1RD0LA_1RE0RB_0LA0LF_0LD1LF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LE_0RC---_1RD0LA_1RE0RB_0LA0LF_0LD1LF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape's words and the base-4 schedule of the head's trips are identified and measured to 1.5·1010 steps; no rule is proved yet beyond the generated ones.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 66,928 cells have been visited and 22,316 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.056). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.468).

claims.title: The block structure
claims.text: At each visit of the left end the tape is a list of blocks of 100 separated by 1010; per visit the blocks lose 4, 12, 48, 192, 768 words (position by position), the last ones grow; no halt in 1.5·10<sup>10</sup> steps.

claims.title: The base-4 schedule
claims.text: In the turn points of the run, trips to the nearest wall repeat four times for each trip one wall further, as the digits of a base-4 counter.

claims.title: Shift rules, for any number of copies
claims.text: D runs right over the words 100 of a block (turning them into 001), F runs left over them (into 010), E runs left over separators 10, B runs right over 001; each for every number of copies and any tape around.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts exactly at A>0 1 or D>1 1; whether the refill of exhausted blocks produces one is not worked out.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this machine builds a list of blocks of the word 100 and runs its head through them on a base-4 schedule, so the blocks shrink at rates 4, 12, 48, 192, … per visit of the left end. This page runs the real machine and shows the blocks.

facts.text: The blocks' shrink rates, level by level.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.056). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.468).
After 109 steps the tape spans 66,928 cells (50 left of the start, 49,870 right), with a density of 1s of 0.333.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Blocks that shrink at rates 4, 12, 48, …
html: At each visit of the left end (state E) the tape is a list of blocks of the word 100 separated by 1010 (0 is an empty block):

Down the columns, the first block loses 4 words per visit, the second 12, the third 48, then 192, 768. Between two such visits the head shuttles between the walls and the right end on a base-4 schedule: four short trips for each trip one wall further, and so on. Each trip moves a wall by one word.
The machine halts exactly when A reads a 0 followed by a 1 or D reads a 1 followed by a 1. Whether the way exhausted blocks are refilled ever produces that is the open question.

summary: Blocks of the word 100 separated by 1010; the head's trips follow a base-4 schedule, so per visit of the left end the blocks lose 4, 12, 48, 192, 768 words; the refill rule and halting are not worked out.
